metadata.title: 343 Companies Report $28.5 Billion In Trump Tariff Refunds. Here's Where The Money Is Going.

content.text:
Hundreds of major U.S. companies have reported $28.5 billion in tariff refunds received or expected after the Supreme Court overturned President Donald Trump's emergency tariffs, with the money being used for everything from lowering business costs to repaying customers and calculating corporate bonuses.
A new database published Thursday by ProPublica identifies 343 publicly traded companies reporting refunds, including FedEx, Walmart, Apple, Ford and Target. The investigation examined corporate financial disclosures to identify how much companies had recovered or expected to receive.
FedEx topped the list with $3.3 billion, followed by Walmart at $2.9 billion, Apple at $2.2 billion, Ford at $1.3 billion and Target at $994 million. Nike, Home Depot and Amazon were also among the largest recipients or expected beneficiaries.
The $28.5 billion includes both money already recovered and anticipated refunds, rather than confirmed cash payments to all 343 companies.
Walmart disclosed in its quarterly filing that it received approximately $2.9 billion in refunds during the quarter ended July 31. The retailer recorded the payments as a reduction in its cost of sales and said a significant portion was invested in pricing and other measures intended to offset costs for customers.
Target also recorded substantial financial benefits. In its third-quarter earnings released Wednesday, the retailer reported $301 million in pretax tariff refund benefits, contributing $228 million to net earnings and adding 50 cents to earnings per share.
Target's total recognized tariff refund benefits reached approximately $1.3 billion during the first nine months of 2026, exceeding the older $994 million figure included in ProPublica's database.
FedEx, meanwhile, reported receiving $3.3 billion in cash refunds through September 30. The shipping company also recorded $2.7 billion in estimated obligations to return money to customers who paid the original tariff charges.
FedEx and UPS have established online systems allowing eligible customers to track and request refunds.
Other companies are handling the money differently.
A separate ProPublica investigation published Monday identified at least nine companies whose tariff refunds were reflected in corporate bonus arrangements.
Stanley Black & Decker, which reported at least $298 million in refunds, disclosed that some of the financial gain was offset by costs related to incentive compensation.
TJX, the parent company of TJ Maxx and Marshalls, received $331 million in refunds and was also among the companies identified in the investigation.
